images.caption: Figure 2:Overview of LayoutRecall.In each editing roundtt, our model generates the target imageItI_{t}that follows the target layoutBtB_{t}. The current imageIt−1I_{t-1}and its layoutBt−1B_{t-1}serve as local context, while the Box-Surface Latent Memory (BSLM) provides long-term context. Relevant memory is retrieved from BSLM and injected into the FLUX.2 editor through Geometry-Aligned Memory Conditioning (GAMC). OnceItI_{t}is generated, its observations are written back into BSLM.

Figure 3:Writing and retrieval in BSLM.A ray from the camera through an image token’s center maps it to a cell on its object’s 3D box surface. Retrieval is performed in the same way with the target camera and box layout.
Figure 4:Qualitative results of single-round editing.The prompts for the two added objects are “an orange traffic cone” and “a stack of wooden pallets”.

Figure 5:Qualitative results of multi-round editing.SeeThrough3D regenerates the target while completely discarding the original content. BoxCtrl replaces the scene with an empty background. With its long-term memory, LayoutRecall restores the toy car previously hidden by the moved sofa in round 7 and the plant previously hidden by the added cabinet in round 8 (yellow circles).

Figure 6:Qualitative ablation results.When the camera returns in round 3, only the full model restores the orange ball (yellow circle). Without BLC-Fourier, the stone table and the bike are distorted.

Figure 7:Additional qualitative results of multi-round editing.In round 3 (yellow circles), unlike the single-round editor Thinking-in-Boxes[5], LayoutRecall restores the appearance of the orange ball, which was occluded by the car, and of the streetlight and the tree, which were out of view.
